headline: Fifth Circuit pick Todd Butler cites role in voiding Mississippi vote
dek: Trump's pick for the Fifth Circuit lists his amicus work against Mississippi's voter-approved medical cannabis initiative among his most significant cases.
key_points: Todd Butler, nominated to the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, listed his work on the 2021 case that struck down Mississippi's Initiative 65 in his Senate questionnaire.
Butler was lead amicus counsel for the Mississippi State Department of Health, which argued the medical cannabis measure should never have been on the ballot.
The Senate Judiciary Committee heard his nomination on 10 November; Republicans are moving to confirm judges before Democrats take the Senate majority in January.
The Fifth Circuit hears federal appeals from Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi, where hemp, medical cannabis and rescheduling disputes are all live.
body: President Donald Trump's nominee for a seat on the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit has put his role in overturning Mississippi's voter-approved medical cannabis initiative near the top of his legal record. In his Senate Judiciary Committee questionnaire, Todd Butler, a Mississippi employment lawyer and managing partner at Phelps Dunbar's Flowood office, lists the Initiative 65 case among the significant litigated matters he has handled.

The Judiciary Committee heard Butler's nomination on 10 November. Marijuana Moment reported on 13 November that a letter from former law clerks supporting him also cites the case. If confirmed, Butler would replace Judge Leslie Southwick, who is taking senior status.
## What Butler did in the Initiative 65 case

Mississippi voters approved Initiative 65 in November 2020 to create a medical cannabis programme. A court challenge argued the measure had not qualified properly for the ballot. In his questionnaire, Butler says he served as lead amicus counsel for the Mississippi State Department of Health in that case, In re Initiative Measure No. 65, from 2020 to 2021.

The Mississippi Supreme Court agreed with his client's reading of the state constitution and held that the initiative should never have gone on the ballot, Butler writes. His brief urged the court to rely only on the text of the constitution's initiative section and to reject a purpose-based reading. The ruling voided the measure. Lawmakers later passed the Mississippi Medical Cannabis Act, and the questionnaire shows Butler went on to give talks to employers and municipal officials in 2022 on the new law and its workplace implications.
> A judge's record on a cannabis ballot fight says nothing certain about future rulings, but nominees choose which cases to highlight, and this one made the list.
## Why the Fifth Circuit matters to cannabis

The Fifth Circuit hears federal appeals from Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi. All three are now cannabis battlegrounds. Texas is weighing hemp THC rules and a bigger medical programme in its 2027 session, Louisiana runs a medical programme, and Mississippi's medical market is four years old. Federal fights over hemp, state licensing and the DEA's registration system can all end up before regional appeals courts, and a lifetime appointment shapes those rulings for decades.

Butler's record otherwise centres on employment and municipal law. His questionnaire lists work defending local officials in First Amendment cases and many talks on federal employment law. Josh Blackman, a conservative law professor writing at the Volokh Conspiracy, criticised the questionnaire as thin for a Fifth Circuit nominee and questioned the timeline, noting Sen. Roger Wicker contacted Butler about the seat in June, three months before Southwick announced he would step back.

The questionnaire sets out a short timeline. Wicker contacted Butler on 29 June about a possible vacancy, and he spoke with Hyde-Smith the next day. He interviewed with the White House Counsel's Office on 13 July, and Trump called him on 1 October to say he would be nominated. Southwick publicly announced on 28 September that he would take senior status, Blackman noted, which is the gap he questioned. Blackman also pointed out that Butler joined the Federalist Society only in 2016 and has held no leadership role in it.

Butler appeared on the first panel of the 10 November hearing, ahead of three district court nominees for Tennessee, North Dakota and Louisiana, according to committee chair Chuck Grassley's opening statement. Grassley described all four as exceptional attorneys.

Butler was introduced to the committee by Mississippi's senators, Wicker and Cindy Hyde-Smith, who said in a joint statement that they enthusiastically support him. Senate Republicans are looking to fast-track White House judicial nominees before Democrats take the majority, the Magnolia Tribune reported.

The calendar is tight. Democrats will hold at least 55 Senate seats in the new Congress, NBC News projected, and one of those flips came in Mississippi itself: the Associated Press called Hyde-Smith's race for Democrat Scott Colom on 11 November. Colom, a district attorney, has backed alternatives to incarceration for non-violent drug offences, though he has not set out a position on federal legalisation. Hyde-Smith has opposed federal cannabis reform, including rescheduling and banking bills, The Marijuana Herald noted.

Watch for a Judiciary Committee vote on Butler and whether the Senate confirms him before the new Congress is sworn in. In the Fifth Circuit's states, watch the Texas legislature's 2027 session for hemp and medical cannabis bills that could later face court challenges.
